claims.text: A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, and a protein consists of one or more polypeptides; because the order of amino acids is coded for by a gene, a change in the gene can change the polypeptide. For example, a polypeptide of 146 amino acids is coded for by 146 × 3 = 438 bases, before a stop codon is counted.

claims.text: In transcription the double strand of a gene unwinds over a short length, one strand (the template strand) acts as the pattern, free RNA nucleotides pair with its exposed bases by complementary base pairing (A in DNA pairs with U in RNA, T with A, C with G, G with C), and RNA polymerase joins them into a single strand of mRNA. The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, not a copy of it, and has the same base order as the other DNA strand except that U replaces T. It then leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore.

claims.text: Messenger RNA carries the code of a gene as a series of codons from the DNA in the nucleus to a ribosome; transfer RNA is a single strand folded so that one end carries an anticodon and the other end carries one particular amino acid; a ribosome is made of ribosomal RNA and protein, has two parts (a small and a large subunit), holds the mRNA and two tRNA molecules at a time and joins the amino acids with peptide bonds.

claims.text: In translation the mRNA binds to a ribosome; a tRNA whose anticodon is complementary to the start codon AUG (anticodon UAC) brings methionine; further tRNA molecules pair with successive codons, the ribosome joins the amino acids by peptide bonds and moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and at a stop codon the polypeptide is released. The order of codons on the mRNA decides the order of amino acids.
